questions.stem: Which source of energy drives the water cycle?
options: Wind blowing over the sea
Light from the Moon
Heat from the Sun
Cold air from the clouds

explain.why: Wind moves clouds, but it does not give the heat that changes water into water vapour.
The Moon gives very little light and no useful heat.
Cold air takes heat away. It cannot make water evaporate.

solution: The Sun's heat makes water evaporate, which starts the water cycle.

questions.stem: What is the name of the process that changes water from a pond into water vapour?
options: Condensation
Freezing
Melting
Evaporation

explain.why: Condensation changes water vapour into liquid water.
Freezing changes a liquid into a solid.
Melting changes a solid into a liquid.

solution: Liquid water changing into water vapour is evaporation.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes water vapour?
options: Small pieces of ice in the air
Water as an invisible gas
Tiny drops of water that we can see
Smoke made when water is heated

explain.why: Ice is solid water, not water vapour.
Tiny visible drops are liquid water, as in clouds and mist.
Smoke is made of solid bits from burning things.

solution: Water vapour is a gas. We cannot see it.

questions.stem: What happens to water vapour when it cools high up in the air?
options: It evaporates again and rises higher
It melts into a block of ice up high
It becomes smoke and drifts away with the wind
It condenses into tiny water droplets

explain.why: Evaporation needs heat and changes liquid water into water vapour.
Melting is for solids.
Water vapour does not turn into smoke.

solution: Cooling water vapour condenses into tiny water droplets.

questions.stem: Look at the cloud in the picture. What is it made up of?
options: tiny droplets of water
water vapour only
smoke from factories
pieces of cotton-like dust

explain.why: Water vapour is invisible. We see clouds because of the liquid droplets.
Smoke is not what clouds are made of.
Clouds have no dust fibres like cotton.

solution: Clouds are tiny water droplets formed by condensation.

questions.stem: Why does rain fall from a cloud?
options: The cloud has used up all of its water vapour
The droplets join and get too heavy to stay up
The Sun pulls the water down to the ground
The wind turns the whole cloud into solid ice

explain.why: Rain is made from the water droplets in the cloud.
The Sun gives heat. It does not pull water down.
Wind moves clouds, but it does not make rain by itself.

solution: Droplets join into bigger drops. When they are too heavy they fall as rain.

questions.stem: Hot water is covered with a plastic sheet. After some time, drops of water form under the sheet. What do the drops show?
options: The plastic sheet has made new water from air
Water vapour has changed to liquid water
The hot water has frozen onto the sheet
The water has become heavier and fallen

explain.why: Water is not made by plastic. It comes from the bowl.
Hot water does not freeze.
The water has only changed from vapour to liquid.

solution: Water vapour from the hot water cooled at the sheet and condensed into drops.

R is rain falling from the cloud.

solution: Condensation happens in the cloud, at Q.

questions.stem: Why does the Earth not run out of water even though water evaporates all the time?
options: The Sun makes a lot of new water every day
New water is made inside the clouds each day
Only a very little water evaporates from the sea
The water keeps moving around sea, air and land

explain.why: The Sun only gives heat. It does not make water.
Clouds are formed from water that evaporated earlier.
A lot of water evaporates, but it returns as rain.

solution: The water cycle moves the same water around again and again.

questions.stem: Which of the following do plants use water for?
options: To keep warm at night
To make their food
To make sunlight
To make soil

explain.why: Water is not used by plants as a blanket.
Plants cannot make sunlight.
Plants do not make soil from water.

solution: Plants use water, light and carbon dioxide to make food.

questions.stem: A plant was not watered for many days. Its leaves became soft and drooped. What is the most likely reason?
options: The plant had too much water
The plant had too much sunlight
The plant grew too many roots
The plant lost water

explain.why: A plant with too much water does not droop like this.
Too much light does not make leaves droop by itself.
More roots would take in more water.

solution: Plants droop, or wilt, when they lose water.

questions.stem: On a hot day, what does the body make to help it cool down?
options: Urine
Saliva
Mucus
Sweat

explain.why: Urine is made to remove waste.
Saliva is made in the mouth to help with eating.
Mucus lines the nose and throat.

solution: Sweat is mostly water. It helps to cool the body.

questions.stem: About how much of the human body is water?
options: About one tenth of it
Exactly all of it
More than half of it
Almost none of it

explain.why: The body has much more water than this.
The body also has solid parts such as bones.
Water is a large part of the body.

solution: Over half of the human body is water.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a way to save water at home?
options: Leaving the tap running while washing dishes
Flushing the toilet many times for no reason
Turning off the tap while brushing teeth
Washing a car with a running hose

explain.why: A running tap wastes a lot of water.
Each flush uses clean water.
A hose uses much more water than a bucket.

solution: Turning off the tap stops water from being wasted.

questions.stem: Which action pollutes the water in a river?
options: Using a bin for rubbish
Picking up litter near the river bank
Planting trees along the river bank to hold soil
Pouring used cooking oil down a drain

explain.why: Rubbish in a bin does not reach the river.
Removing litter keeps the river clean.
Trees do not pollute the river.

solution: Used oil flows to rivers and the sea and pollutes the water.

questions.stem: A factory pours chemicals into a river. What is likely to happen to the fish in the river?
options: Many of them may die
They will grow bigger
They will move faster
Nothing will happen to them

explain.why: Chemicals harm living things.
Polluted water does not make fish faster.
Harmful chemicals can poison fish.

solution: Chemicals in water can poison fish and plants.

questions.stem: Which of the following helps to keep water clean?
options: Pouring oil into the sea
Putting rubbish into a bin
Washing paint brushes in a pond
Throwing rubbish into a drain

explain.why: Oil spills harm the sea.
Paint pollutes the water.
Drains lead to rivers and the sea.

solution: Rubbish in a bin cannot reach the water.

questions.stem: What is NEWater?
options: Used water cleaned so that it can be used again
Sea water that is sold with its salt left in
Water that comes from a brand new tap
Rain water collected from roofs and drains

explain.why: Salt would make it unfit to drink.
NEWater is not named for a tap.
NEWater is made from used water, not directly from rain.

solution: NEWater is treated used water.

questions.stem: Why should we not drink water straight from a dirty river?
options: It has no real water in it at all
It may have germs that make us ill
It makes our teeth much stronger
It is too heavy for our bodies to drink

explain.why: River water is water, but it may be unsafe.
Dirty water does not help teeth.
Dirty water is not heavier in a way that matters.

solution: Dirty water can carry germs that cause diseases.

questions.stem: Which of the following wastes water?
options: Using a basin of water to wash vegetables
Letting the tap run while washing plates
Using a bucket of water to wash a bicycle
Watering the plants with water used for rinsing rice

explain.why: A basin uses less water than a running tap.
A bucket limits the water used.
Reusing water saves clean water.

solution: A running tap wastes water that could be saved.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a water habitat?
options: A desert
A hole in a tree
A pond
A termite mound

explain.why: A desert is very dry land.
A hole in a tree is on land.
A termite mound is on land.

solution: A pond is full of water and animals and plants live in it.

questions.stem: The table shows how much water is used by some ways of washing. Which way uses the least water?
options: Brushing teeth with the tap on
Brushing teeth with the tap off
Washing the face with the tap on
Washing the face with a basin

explain.why: This used 12 litres, the most.
This used 8 litres.
This used 2 litres, more than 1 litre.

solution: Tap off: 1 litre. This is the smallest amount.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the water cycle. What happens at Q?
options: Water vapour cools and forms tiny droplets
Tiny droplets of water change into ice
Rain water flows into the river
Water from the sea changes into water vapour

explain.why: No freezing is part of this picture.
Water flowing down is run-off, not what happens in the cloud.
That is evaporation, which happens as water rises from the sea.

solution: Q is the cloud, where condensation takes place.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the water cycle. Which two letters show stages in which water changes its state?
options: P and Q
S and Q
R and S
R and P

explain.why: Q shows water flowing as a liquid.
S and Q show water falling and flowing as a liquid, so the state is not changing.
S shows water falling as a liquid.

solution: R is evaporation and P is condensation. In both, water changes between gas and liquid.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the water cycle. Which letter shows the stage that needs heat from the Sun?
options: P
S
R
Q

explain.why: P is condensation, which happens when water vapour cools.
R is run-off, which is driven by the slope of the land.
Q is rain, which falls because of its weight.

solution: Evaporation needs the Sun's heat. It is shown by S.

questions.stem: Over a large lake, the Sun's heat is blocked for many weeks by thick smoke. What is most likely to happen to the rain over the lake?
options: There will be more rain
There will be less rain
The rain will be the same
The rain will turn salty

explain.why: Less heat means less water evaporates, so fewer clouds form.
The rain depends on how much water evaporates.
Rain does not take up salt from the lake.

solution: Less heat means less evaporation and fewer clouds.

questions.stem: Look at the model of the water cycle. Why are ice cubes placed on the plastic sheet?
options: They cool the vapour so that drops form
They make the plastic sheet thicker and stronger
They stop water vapour from forming
They heat the water vapour in the bowl

explain.why: The sheet stays the same thickness.
Vapour forms from the hot water below.
Ice takes heat away.

solution: Cold ice cools the sheet, so the vapour condenses to drops.

questions.stem: Drops of water appear on the outside of a cold can in a warm room. Where did most of this water come from?
options: Water made by the cold can
Water that came out of the can's metal
Water vapour in the air
Water that leaked through the can

explain.why: The can cannot make water.
Metal does not hold water.
The can is not leaking. The drops form even on a sealed can.

solution: Water vapour in the warm air cooled at the can and condensed into drops.

questions.stem: The bar graph shows the amount of rain in a town in six months. How much more rain fell in May than in March?
options: 60 mm
160 mm
40 mm
100 mm

explain.why: This is the rain in March alone.
This adds the two months instead of finding the difference.
100 mm is the rain in May alone, not the difference.

solution: May is 100 mm and March is 60 mm. 100 - 60 = 40 mm.

options: Water vapour dropped into the pond
The Sun's heat made water evaporate
The water condensed into rain in the pond
The pond made more water vapour at night

explain.why: That would raise the level.
Condensation does not remove water from a pond.
The level fell steadily during the whole time.

solution: With no rain, water lost through evaporation lowers the level.

The river was the cleanest place at B
Something harmful may have entered near B
The river flows upwards to A

explain.why: There are fewer fish near the factory.
Place B has the fewest fish.
The table says nothing about the flow.

solution: Fish fall from 24 at A to 9 at B, so pollution near B is likely.

options: Showering
Laundry
Flushing
Cooking

explain.why: Laundry is the second highest, not the highest.
Flushing uses less water than showering.
Cooking uses the least water of the four.

solution: Showering uses 120 litres, the most.

questions.stem: Why can people not drink sea water straight from the sea?
options: It has no water in it
It is too warm to drink
It has too much salt in it
It has too little salt in it

explain.why: Sea water is mostly water.
Temperature is not the problem.
The salt is the problem.

solution: The salt in sea water makes it unfit to drink.

questions.stem: Why do countries store rain water in reservoirs?
options: To stop clouds from forming
To make the sea salty
To keep the water from evaporating at all
To keep fresh water for later use

explain.why: Storing rain does not affect clouds.
Reservoirs have nothing to do with sea salt.
Some water still evaporates from reservoirs.

solution: A reservoir gives a store of fresh water.

questions.stem: A factory pours oily waste into a river. Which is a likely result for the river?
options: The river gets more oxygen for the fish
Less clean water is left for living things to use
Rain stops falling over the river
The river water becomes cleaner

explain.why: Oil on water makes it harder for fish to live.
Pollution in a river does not stop the rain.
Waste makes water dirtier, not cleaner.

solution: Water pollution means less clean water for living things.

questions.stem: Why does an oil spill harm sea birds and fish?
options: The oil makes the animals grow much faster than usual
The oil coats animals and blocks air from the water
The oil makes the sea water much warmer
The oil makes the sea water far too salty

explain.why: Oil does not help living things grow.
The harm is from coating and blocking air.
Oil does not add salt to the sea.

solution: Oil sticks to feathers and gills and stops air from reaching the water.

questions.stem: Which action by a community would do most to reduce litter in a river?
options: Telling people to drink much more water each day
Using more fertiliser on the farms nearby
Building much taller houses along the river
Putting out bins and teaching people to use them

explain.why: Drinking water does not remove litter.
More fertiliser makes pollution worse.
This does not stop litter.

solution: Bins and good habits keep litter out of drains and rivers.

questions.stem: Why is it unsafe to let sewage flow into a river without treating it?
options: It makes the river flow backwards
It stops the Sun from heating the river
It makes the water too clean to drink
It carries germs that spread diseases

explain.why: Sewage does not change the direction of flow.
Sewage does not block the Sun's heat.
Sewage makes the water dirtier.

solution: Untreated sewage has germs that cause illness.

questions.stem: A celery stalk is placed in red water for one day. Red lines are seen inside the stalk. What does this show?
options: The stalk gives out water from its cut end
The stalk makes red water
Water moves down from the leaves
Water moves up through the stalk

explain.why: The water entered the stalk.
The colour came from outside.
The red colour shows the water going up from the cut end.

solution: Plants carry water up through tubes in the stem.

questions.stem: On a very hot afternoon a plant wilts, but it stands up again after being watered. Why did it wilt?
options: Its leaves made far too much food to hold
It lost water faster than the roots took it in
Its stem grew too long to stand up
Its roots took in far too much water

explain.why: Making food does not make a plant droop.
Stem length does not change in one afternoon.
Too much water does not make a plant wilt.

solution: A plant wilts when it loses more water than it takes in.

questions.stem: On a hot day we sweat a lot. How does sweating help the body?
options: Sweat stops the blood from moving
Sweat makes the skin thicker and tougher
Sweat adds heat to the skin
Sweat takes heat away as it dries

explain.why: Blood keeps moving.
Sweat does not change the thickness of skin.
Evaporating sweat takes heat away.

solution: Sweat evaporates and takes heat away, so the body cools.

questions.stem: Which job does water do inside the human body?
options: It makes the bones hard and strong
It makes the air that the lungs breathe
It stops us from ever feeling thirsty
It forms most of the blood that carries food

explain.why: Bones are hardened by other materials, not water.
Water does not make air.
Drinking water does this, but it is not a job of water in the body.

solution: Blood is mostly water and carries food and oxygen.

questions.stem: Which two actions both help to save water?
options: Washing a car with a hose and leaving the tap on
Washing a car with a bucket and watering plants with rinse water
Washing a car with a bucket and leaving a tap dripping
Watering plants with rinse water and using a hose to wash the path

explain.why: Both waste water.
A dripping tap wastes water.
A hose wastes water.

solution: A bucket uses less water than a hose. Rinse water is reused.

questions.stem: Most of the Earth is covered with water. Why must people still save water?
options: Water gets used up and is never replaced
Only a little of it is fresh water we can use
Fresh water cannot evaporate or fall as rain
Water is made only in the sea and then lost

explain.why: Rain replaces water, but clean fresh water is still limited.
All water can evaporate.
Water moves in the water cycle.

solution: Fresh water is a small part of all the water on Earth.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the water cycle. At which letter does water lose heat as it changes into tiny droplets?
options: S
R
P
Q

explain.why: S is water vapour rising as it gains heat.
P is rain falling.
Q is river water flowing.

solution: Water vapour loses heat and condenses in the cloud, R.

options: April
May
June
March

explain.why: From April to May the level changed by 2 m.
From May to June the level fell.
From February to March the level rose by only 2 m.

solution: March to April: 8 m to 14 m. This is the biggest rise.

questions.stem: A student wants more drops to form under the plastic sheet in the same time. Which change would help?
options: Take the plastic sheet off the bowl
Use cooler water in the bowl
Put a warm cloth on the sheet
Put more ice on top of the sheet

explain.why: Vapour would escape instead of condensing.
Cooler water makes less water vapour.
A warm sheet cools the vapour less.

solution: More ice cools the sheet more, so more vapour condenses.

options: Water flows up the river at S
Tiny droplets change into water vapour at R
Water vapour turns into tiny droplets at Q
Water changes from gas to liquid at P

explain.why: River water flows down to the sea.
At R the water is already falling as a liquid.
At P, liquid water changes into water vapour.

solution: P is evaporation, Q is condensation, R is rain, S is run-off.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the water cycle. Which stages need the water to be cooled?
options: Only the stage at P
Only the stage at S
The stages at R and S
The stages at P and Q

explain.why: P needs heat, not cooling.
R is rain falling. It does not need cooling.
Water gains heat to evaporate. It does not need to be cooled.

solution: Condensation, at S, needs cooling. Evaporation, at P, needs heat.

questions.stem: Set-ups A and B each have a bowl of the same hot water and a plastic sheet. The only difference is the ice on A. After 10 minutes, which set-up has more drops under its sheet and why?
options: A, because the ice cools the vapour more
They are the same, because the water is the same
A, because the ice adds water to the sheet
B, because it is warmer under the sheet

explain.why: The sheet is colder in A, so more vapour condenses.
The ice does not add water under the sheet.
A warmer sheet cools the vapour less.

solution: The colder sheet in A makes more water vapour condense into drops.

questions.stem: Water is boiled in a pot with a lid. Drops of water form under the lid and fall back into the pot. Which part of the water cycle does the lid most resemble?
options: The Sun that heats the water
The sea where water evaporates
A cold place high in the air
A river that carries water

explain.why: The Sun is like the stove, not the lid.
The sea is where water evaporates, like the hot pot.
A river flows. The lid does not.

solution: The cool lid acts like the cold air, so vapour condenses on it.

questions.stem: Why do clouds form high above the ground rather than on the ground?
options: Water vapour only forms in high air
Water vapour is too heavy to stay low
Rising air cools, so the vapour condenses
The Sun heats the air more and more at the top

explain.why: Water vapour forms from the sea and land below.
Water vapour is light and rises.
The air gets cooler, not hotter, as it rises.

solution: The vapour rises into cooler air and condenses into droplets.

questions.stem: Tiny droplets in a cloud stay in the air, but raindrops fall. What is the main difference?
options: Raindrops are bigger and heavier
Raindrops have salt in them
Raindrops are warmer than the droplets
Raindrops are made of water vapour

explain.why: Rain is fresh water.
Temperature does not decide this.
Water vapour is a gas and cannot fall as drops.

solution: Many tiny droplets join into a drop that is too heavy to stay up.

questions.stem: A pond gets water only from rain. In a month with no rain, the pond becomes smaller. Which is the main reason?
options: The rain stopped the water from evaporating
More water evaporated than was gained
The pond made more clouds for itself
The water condensed and left the pond

explain.why: No rain fell.
A pond does not make clouds by itself.
Condensation does not take water out of a pond.

solution: No rain came in, and water kept evaporating.

questions.stem: The table shows the water going into a reservoir and the water used from it each month. In which month did the reservoir lose the most water overall?
options: April
January
February
March

explain.why: In April the reservoir gained water.
In January the loss was 15 million m3. In February it was 20.
In March the reservoir gained water.

solution: Feb: 30 - 50 = -20. Jan: 40 - 55 = -15. March and April gain water.

questions.stem: A tap leaks and wastes 4 litres of water every hour. How much water does it waste in 2 days?
options: 192 litres
48 litres
8 litres
96 litres

explain.why: This is only 12 hours' worth.
This is only 2 hours' worth.
This is for 1 day only. 4 x 24 = 96.

solution: 2 days = 48 hours. 4 x 48 = 192 litres.

questions.stem: Which statement about untreated used water flowing into a river is correct?
options: It can make the water unsafe and harm living things
It makes the river water cleaner and safer for fish
It is safe because the river flows to the sea
It affects only the colour of the river and nothing else

explain.why: Untreated used water adds dirt and germs.
Pollution spreads with the flowing water.
It can also carry germs and harmful chemicals.

solution: Used water carries germs and chemicals.

questions.stem: How does NEWater help a country that has little land to store rain water?
options: It makes more rain fall on the land
It turns the sea water into new rivers
It gives fresh water made from used water
It stops water from ever being used up

explain.why: NEWater does not change the rain.
NEWater is made from used water.
Water still needs to be treated and used carefully.

solution: Used water is cleaned and used again, adding to the water supply.

questions.stem: Which action helps to keep the fresh water of rivers and lakes clean?
options: Washing rubbish into the stream
Throwing litter into the canal
Treating used water before it flows back to the river
Pouring used cooking oil down the drain

explain.why: Rubbish pollutes the water.
Litter pollutes the water.
Oil pollutes the water.

solution: Treating used water removes dirt before it reaches the river.

questions.stem: Three plants were kept as shown in the table, and each had enough air. Which plant could make food?
options: Plant Z only
Plant Y only
Plant X only
All three plants

explain.why: Plant Z has water but no light.
Plant Y has light but no water.
Making food needs both light and water.

solution: Plants need water and light to make food.

questions.stem: After running a race, a child drinks water. Which is the best reason for this?
options: To turn sweat into blood at once
To replace water lost as sweat
To make the muscles grow bigger
To make the heart stop beating fast

explain.why: Sweat is not turned into blood.
Muscles do not grow from one drink.
Drinking water does not stop the heart rate.

solution: Sweat is mostly water. Replacing it helps cooling and blood flow.

questions.stem: A pond dried up in a long hot spell, and all the fish in it died. Why?
options: The fish were too heavy for the dry pond
The fish evaporated into the air
The fish could no longer make clouds
The fish had no water to live in and take in oxygen from

explain.why: Weight is not why they died.
Fish do not turn into water vapour.
Fish do not make clouds.

solution: Without water, fish lose their habitat and cannot take in oxygen.

questions.stem: After a hot shower, the bathroom mirror is covered with tiny drops of water. Why did the drops form on the mirror?
options: The mirror was heated by the shower
The mirror soaked up water from the walls
The mirror made new water by itself
The cool mirror cooled the vapour

explain.why: A cooler mirror causes the drops.
The drops come from the air.
A mirror cannot make water.

solution: Vapour cooled at the cooler mirror and condensed into drops.

questions.stem: Sea water is salty, but rain water is not. What is the best explanation?
options: The salt stays behind as water evaporates
The clouds remove the salt with the wind
The sea water loses its salt when it rains
The salt turns into water vapour too

explain.why: Wind does not remove salt.
Salt remains in the sea.
Salt stays in the sea.

solution: Only the water changes into vapour. The salt stays in the sea.

questions.stem: The bar graph shows the rain in six months. What is the total rain in March and April?
options: 70 mm
60 mm
10 mm
130 mm

explain.why: This is April alone.
This is March alone.
This is the difference, not the total.

solution: March 60 mm + April 70 mm = 130 mm.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the water cycle. In which stage does water move through the air as a gas?
options: The arrow marked R
The arrow marked P
The arrow marked Q
The cloud marked S

explain.why: R is the river, where the water is a liquid.
Q is the rain, which falls as liquid drops.
The cloud holds liquid droplets, not a gas.

solution: Water rises as water vapour, which is a gas.

questions.stem: A glass of river water looks clear, but a child still becomes ill after drinking it. What is the best explanation?
options: The river must have been far too cold to drink
Harmful germs or chemicals can still be in it
Clear water cannot be digested by the body
Clear water always has too little oxygen

explain.why: Cold water does not cause this illness.
Water is not digested.
Clear water does not mean low oxygen.

solution: Germs are too small to see, and some harmful chemicals dissolve in water.

questions.stem: A family collects the water used to rinse vegetables and uses it to water plants. What is the main benefit?
options: The rinse water becomes fresh water
Less clean water is needed from the tap
The vegetables are cleaned without water
The plants need no light any more

explain.why: Rinse water is not made fresh.
Water is still used to rinse them.
Plants always need light.

solution: Reusing water means less tap water is used.

questions.stem: Which two parts of the water cycle bring water into a lake?
options: Rain falling and evaporation from the lake
Evaporation and condensation
Rain falling and rivers flowing in
Condensation and evaporation from the land

explain.why: Evaporation takes water away from the lake.
These take water into the air or form clouds.
Neither brings water into the lake.

solution: Rain and rivers add water. Evaporation removes water.

questions.stem: A tank holds 600 litres of water. Each week it gains 150 litres from rain and 200 litres are used. How much water is in the tank after 3 weeks?
options: 750 litres
150 litres
450 litres
600 litres

explain.why: This adds the 50 litres each week instead of taking it away.
This is one week of rain only.
The amount in the tank changes each week.

solution: Each week: 150 - 200 = -50 litres. After 3 weeks: 600 - 150 = 450 litres.

questions.stem: Why is it important to save water even in a country with plenty of rain?
options: Clean water is costly to make and limited
The Sun makes water disappear from the Earth
Water in taps is not part of the water cycle
Rain water is always far too salty to use

explain.why: Water stays in the water cycle.
It is part of the same cycle.
Rain water is fresh.

solution: Treating and supplying clean water is costly, and clean fresh water is limited.

questions.stem: Look at the picture of the water cycle. At which letter do drops of liquid water reach the ground?
options: P
R
S
Q

explain.why: P is water rising as a gas.
R is the river, where water is already on the land.
Q is the cloud, whose droplets are too light to fall.

solution: Rain falls as liquid drops, at S.

questions.stem: Which process changes liquid water at the surface of a puddle into water vapour?
options: Condensation
Freezing
Evaporation
Melting

explain.why: Condensation changes water vapour into liquid water, the opposite change.
Freezing changes liquid water into ice.
Melting changes a solid, such as ice, into liquid water.

solution: Evaporation is the change of liquid water into water vapour at its surface.

questions.stem: Which day is the best for drying wet clothes quickly?
options: A cool day with no wind
A cool and windy day
A hot day with no moving air at all
A hot and windy day

explain.why: Cool, still air gives the slowest drying.
Wind helps, but the cool air slows evaporation.
Heat helps, but there is no wind to carry the vapour away.

solution: Heat and wind both speed up evaporation.

questions.stem: Two identical wet towels are hung in the same sunny spot, one spread out and one folded, as shown. Which towel will dry first?
options: Q, because it is thicker and holds more heat
Both dry at the same time because they are in the same place
Q, because its water is packed close together
P, because more of its water is exposed to the air

explain.why: A thick folded towel hides most of its water from the air, so it dries slower.
The shape matters. The spread towel has a larger exposed surface.
Packed water has less surface in contact with the air.

solution: The spread-out towel P shows a larger surface to the air, so it dries faster.

questions.stem: Which statement about evaporation is correct?
options: It can happen at room temperature
It changes water vapour into liquid water
It happens only when water boils
It happens only when water is in sunlight

explain.why: That is condensation.
Water evaporates at any temperature. Boiling is faster, but evaporation does not wait for it.
Water also evaporates in the shade.

solution: Water evaporates from its surface at any temperature.

questions.stem: After a sunny afternoon, a puddle on a road has gone. Where did the water go?
options: It became vapour and went into the air
It changed into tiny pieces of ice
It was destroyed by the heat of the Sun
It sank down into the hard road

explain.why: The day was hot, so the water did not freeze.
Matter is not destroyed. The water changed state.
A road is hard and does not soak up a puddle.

solution: The water evaporated into water vapour.

questions.stem: Which of the following would increase the rate of evaporation of water in a bowl?
options: Blowing air across the water with a fan
Pouring the water into a narrow tall cup
Moving the bowl to a colder place
Putting a lid on the bowl

explain.why: A narrower surface is smaller, so evaporation is slower.
A colder place slows evaporation.
A lid traps the water vapour above the water.

solution: Moving air carries away water vapour, so evaporation is faster.

questions.stem: Two containers hold the same amount of water and are left in the same place, as shown. Which has less water left after 5 hours?
options: They are the same, as they hold equal water
A, because more of its water touches the air
B, because its water is deeper and stores more heat
B, because its sides are taller

explain.why: Equal amounts of water do not mean equal exposed surface.
Depth does not speed up evaporation. Surface area does.
Tall sides do not help the water evaporate.

solution: A is wider, so it has the larger exposed surface and loses water faster.

questions.stem: Two identical dishes hold the same amount of water. A fan blows over dish A, as shown. Which dries up first?
options: A, because the fan makes the water hotter
B, because still air keeps the water warm
A, because moving air carries the vapour away
They dry up together, as the dishes are the same

explain.why: A fan does not heat the water.
Still air lets vapour build up above the water, so B is slower.
Wind is the one difference, and it speeds up evaporation.

solution: Moving air removes the water vapour at the surface, so A dries first.

questions.stem: Two identical dishes hold the same amount of water. One is in a sunny spot and one in a shady spot, as shown. Which loses more water in 4 hours?
options: B, because the Sun makes its water heavier
A, because the heat of the Sun warms its water
Both lose the same amount of water
B, because the shade is a cooler and calmer place

explain.why: The Sun does not add mass to water.
The Sun makes one dish warmer, so it loses water faster.
Cooler places slow evaporation down.

solution: A is warmer, so its water evaporates faster.

questions.stem: Why do we hang washing in an open, airy place instead of in a closed cupboard?
options: Clothes dry faster because the cupboard has no light
The cupboard adds more water to the clothes
Moving air carries away the vapour, so it dries faster
Moving air makes the water in the clothes boil

explain.why: Light is not what dries the clothes. Moving air and warmth are.
A cupboard does not add water. It just stops the vapour leaving.
Air does not make the water boil.

solution: Wind carries away the water vapour from the clothes.

questions.stem: Where should Mei hang her wet shoes so that they dry quickly?
options: Inside a plastic bag in the shade
Near a sunny window where air can move
In a dark, cold storeroom
Inside a closed shoe cupboard

explain.why: The bag traps the vapour and the shade is cooler.
Cold, still air slows evaporation.
A closed space has no moving air.

solution: A warm, breezy place makes the water evaporate fastest.

questions.stem: Salt is made from seawater in wide, shallow pans left under the Sun. Why are the pans wide and shallow?
options: The salt sinks to the bottom faster in a deep pan
A large surface lets the water evaporate quickly
The water in a wide pan boils faster
A wide pan makes the seawater less salty

explain.why: Depth does not help the water to leave.
Seawater in the pans is not boiled. It evaporates in the Sun.
The amount of salt does not change. Only the water leaves.

solution: More of the water is exposed to the air and the Sun, so it evaporates faster.

questions.stem: Two same pots hold 200 ml of water each. After one day, the pot with a lid has more water left. Why?
options: The lid stops the Sun from heating the water
The lid adds water to the pot
The lid stops the vapour escaping
The lid makes the water too cold to evaporate

explain.why: The pots may be in the same place and heat is not the main cause.
A lid does not add water.
Water at any temperature can evaporate.

solution: With a lid, the water vapour stays trapped, so less water is lost.

questions.stem: Mei wants to find out if wind affects how fast water evaporates. Which two set-ups should she compare?
options: C and D
B and C
A and C
A and B

explain.why: C and D differ in both temperature and amount of water.
B and C differ in both fan and temperature.
A and C differ in temperature, not in wind.

solution: A and B are the same except for the fan.

questions.stem: Which apparatus is best for finding how much water is left in a dish after 3 hours?
options: A thermometer put into the dish
A stopwatch started with the test
A measuring cylinder
A ruler held next to the dish

explain.why: A thermometer measures temperature.
A stopwatch measures time.
A ruler measures length.

solution: A measuring cylinder measures the volume of water.

questions.stem: Each dish had 100 ml of water at first. The bar chart shows the water left after 4 hours. Which dish lost the most water?
options: Q
S
P
R

explain.why: S kept 55 ml, so it lost 45 ml, less than Q.
P kept 70 ml, so it lost 30 ml, less than Q.
R has the tallest bar, which means the most water is left, so it lost the least.

solution: Q has the shortest bar. It kept 40 ml, so it lost 60 ml.

questions.stem: Cup X is left in a hot kitchen and cup Y in a cold room. Both are the same and hold the same amount of water. After one day, which has less water?
options: Neither, because water cannot leave a cup
Cup X, because it is warmer
Cup Y, because it is colder
Both have the same amount of water

explain.why: Water vapour can leave from the open top.
Evaporation is slower in a colder place.
The two places differ in temperature, so the loss differs.

solution: Higher temperature means faster evaporation.

questions.stem: On a hot, dry day the water level in a pond drops. What mainly causes this?
options: Boiling of the pond water
Evaporation of the water
Condensation of the water
Freezing of the pond water

explain.why: A pond is far below boiling temperature.
Condensation would add water, not remove it.
A hot day does not freeze water.

solution: Water evaporates from the pond surface and joins the air as water vapour.

questions.stem: Mrs Tan's kitchen floor is wet. Which action helps the floor dry fastest?
options: Closing all the windows and doors
Closing the curtains to keep the room cool
Switching on a fan to blow air over the floor
Covering the floor with a plastic sheet

explain.why: Closing up stops the air from moving.
A cooler place slows evaporation.
A cover traps the vapour.

solution: Moving air carries away the vapour, so the floor dries faster.

questions.stem: From which part of a dish of water does evaporation take place?
options: The surface of the water
Only the middle of the water
Only the sides of the dish
The bottom of the dish

explain.why: All of the surface can lose water.
The sides do not matter. The surface does.
Vapour leaves at the top where water meets the air.

solution: Water changes into vapour where it meets the air, at the surface.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of evaporation?
options: Droplets form on the outside of a cold glass
Steam turns into drops on a pot lid
Wet footprints on warm ground slowly vanish
Water turns into ice in a freezer

explain.why: That is condensation.
That is condensation.
That is freezing.

solution: The water of the footprints changes into water vapour.

questions.stem: Two identical dishes hold the same amount of water. Dish Q is covered with a lid, as shown. Which loses less water in one day?
options: P, because its water is cooler
P, because the lid draws water out of Q
Both lose the same amount of water
Q, because the vapour cannot escape

explain.why: The uncovered dish is not cooler in any way shown.
A lid does not draw water out.
The lid is the one difference and it slows the loss.

solution: The lid traps the vapour, so Q loses less water.

questions.stem: Ali wants his wet hair to dry quickly. Which is the best way?
options: A hair dryer blowing warm air
Covering it with a plastic cap
Tying it into a tight bun
Sitting in a cold, closed room alone

explain.why: The cap traps the vapour.
A bun hides most of the hair from the air.
Cold, still air is slow.

solution: Warm, moving air makes the water evaporate faster.

questions.stem: Which wet cloth will take the longest time to dry?
options: A cloth spread out under a fan in a warm room
A cloth hung open in a warm, sunny room
A cloth folded up in a closed box in a cool room
A cloth spread out on a hot, windy open balcony

explain.why: Moving air makes it dry fast.
Heat and a wide surface make it dry fast.
This is the fastest way to dry.

solution: Folded, closed in and cool: every factor slows the evaporation.

questions.stem: Why should wet clothes on a line be hung with space between them?
options: The Sun can freeze the clothes if they touch
The clothes weigh less when they are apart
More of each cloth is exposed to moving air
Touching clothes soak up water from each other

explain.why: Heat does not freeze clothes.
The clothes weigh the same however they hang.
Water leaves the clothes into the air. Touching does not add water to them.

solution: Space lets air reach more of the wet surface.

questions.stem: Ali tests how the width of the dish affects the speed of evaporation. Which two set-ups should he compare?
options: A and D
A and B
C and D
B and C

explain.why: A and D differ in width, temperature and fan.
C and D differ in the fan, not in width.
B and C differ in temperature, not in width.

solution: A and B are the same except for the dish width (6 cm and 12 cm).

options: C and D
A and C
B and C
A and B

explain.why: C and D differ in the fan.
A and C differ in both temperature and dish width.
A and B differ in dish width.

solution: B and C differ only in temperature (20 °C and 35 °C).

B has a smaller surface than A, but C is smaller still.

solution: C is the narrowest, so it has the smallest exposed surface.

X, because its line falls more steeply
Both, because the lines start together
Y, because it has more water left

The lines separate, so the rates differ.
More water left means less water evaporated.

solution: X lost 72 ml in 4 hours and Y lost 24 ml, so X evaporated faster.

questions.stem: In salt farms, seawater is led into very wide, shallow ponds in sunny places. Which pair of reasons explains this best?
options: A wide pond holds more water, so there is more salt to collect
A deep pond heats up too fast and the water boils
A big surface and the Sun's heat both speed up evaporation
A shallow pond stops the wind and stores the salt

explain.why: A wide, shallow pond is used so that the water leaves faster, not to hold more of it.
Evaporation, not boiling, removes the water.
Wind helps evaporation and the pond does not stop it.

solution: Wide ponds expose more water, and the Sun warms it.

questions.stem: Wet clothes are hung in a small bathroom with the door and window shut. They dry slowly. Which is the main reason?
options: There is no moving air to carry the vapour away
There is no light to dry the clothes
The clothes weigh more in a small room
Evaporation cannot happen indoors

explain.why: Light itself does not dry clothes.
Weight does not change with the room.
Evaporation happens indoors too, only slower here.

solution: Without moving air, the vapour stays near the clothes.

questions.stem: The same amount of water is poured into a wide dish and a tall, narrow cup and left side by side. After a day, the cup has more water left. Why?
options: The dish makes the water hotter
The cup is taller and the water is deeper
The dish has a larger exposed surface
The cup has less water at first

explain.why: Both are in the same place, so the temperature is the same.
Deeper water does not slow evaporation by being deep. The small surface does.
The question says the amounts are the same.

solution: Evaporation takes place at the surface, so the wider dish loses water faster.

questions.stem: Two identical beakers hold the same amount of water. One is placed near a heater and one in a cool room. Which statement is correct?
options: Only the water near the heater evaporates
The two evaporate at the same rate
The water in the cool room evaporates faster
The water near the heater evaporates faster

explain.why: Water evaporates in a cool room too, only slowly.
The places differ in temperature, so the rates differ.
Heat speeds up evaporation.

solution: Higher temperature gives faster evaporation, but evaporation still happens in the cool room.

questions.stem: Zara says, "Water in an open cup inside a cold refrigerator cannot evaporate." What is the best reply?
options: She is right, because evaporation needs sunlight
She is right, because evaporation only needs boiling
It evaporates faster because it is cold
It does evaporate, but more slowly than in a warm room

explain.why: Sunlight is not needed.
Evaporation takes place at any temperature.
Cold slows evaporation.

solution: Evaporation is slower in the cold but is never zero.

questions.stem: Which statement tells evaporation and boiling apart correctly?
options: Evaporation happens only below 50 °C, and boiling happens only above it
Evaporation needs a fan to start it, and boiling does not
Evaporation makes liquid water, and boiling makes water vapour
Evaporation is at the surface at any temperature, and boiling is throughout the liquid

explain.why: Evaporation also takes place at higher temperatures.
A fan only makes evaporation faster.
Both give water vapour from liquid water.

solution: Evaporation is a surface change at any temperature. Boiling is rapid vapour formation in the whole liquid.

questions.stem: Two identical dishes hold the same amount of water and sit in the same place. Dish Q has a lid. After 6 hours, which is correct?
options: Both have the same amount left
Dish Q has less water left than dish P
Dish P has less water left than dish Q
Dish Q has no water left

explain.why: The lid is the one difference and slows the loss.
The lid keeps the vapour in, so Q loses less.
A covered dish loses water slowly.

solution: The lid traps the vapour, so Q loses less.

questions.stem: Ben pours 100 ml of water each into a tray and a tall cup and leaves them in the Sun for 5 hours. The cup has more water left. What does this show?
options: A tall container keeps the heat of the Sun away from the water
Tall containers make water heavier
Water evaporates only from wide containers
A smaller exposed surface gives slower evaporation

explain.why: Both containers are in the Sun. What differs is the size of the exposed surface.
The mass of water does not depend on the container.
It evaporates from every open container.

solution: The cup's surface is smaller, so less water leaves.

questions.stem: A wet shirt is rolled into a tight ball and another is hung with the sleeves spread. Why does the rolled one dry more slowly?
options: Water cannot evaporate from cloth that is rolled
Most of its water is hidden from the air
The rolled shirt is hotter inside
The spread shirt is heavier so it loses more

explain.why: It evaporates, but only from the outside.
It is not hotter. Its water is just covered.
Weight is not the reason.

solution: The tight roll exposes a small surface, so it dries slowly.

questions.stem: Mei compares a towel spread in the Sun with a towel folded in the shade to see if the area exposed matters. Why is this not a fair test?
options: The towels are both wet at the very start
Both the area and the temperature are different
She is using only two towels in the test
Both towels are made of the same kind of cloth

explain.why: They should both be wet at the start.
Two towels are enough for a comparison.
Equal cloth is correct for a fair test.

solution: Two things differ, so we cannot tell which one caused the difference.

questions.stem: A fan blows over a wet cloth. Why does the cloth dry faster?
options: The fan cools the cloth, so the water evaporates faster
The fan pushes the water out of the cloth
The air carries away the vapour as it forms
The fan heats the water in the cloth

explain.why: A cooler cloth would lose water more slowly, not faster.
The water leaves as vapour, not pushed as liquid.
A fan blows air. It does not heat the water.

solution: Moving air takes away vapour, so more water can evaporate.

questions.stem: Which action would slow down the evaporation of a dish of water the most?
options: Pouring it into a wider dish in a cool room
Covering it with a lid and leaving it in the Sun
Placing it in a cool room and leaving the lid off
Covering it and placing it in a cool room

explain.why: A wider surface speeds up evaporation.
This slows evaporation, but less than doing both.
This slows evaporation, but less than doing both.

solution: A lid and a cool place each slow evaporation. Together they slow it the most.

questions.stem: Dish A is wide and has no fan. Dish B is narrow and has a fan. Both hold the same amount of water. Why can Ali not conclude from this test that wind makes water evaporate faster?
options: Both the dish width and the fan are different
A fan is not needed for a test
Dish A will dry faster, so the fan has no effect
The two dishes hold the same amount of water

explain.why: A fan is a good way to make wind.
The dishes also differ in width, so no conclusion is possible.
This is correct for a fair test.

solution: Two variables are changed, so any difference could be due to either.

questions.stem: After rain, two puddles are the same size. One is in a sunny car park and one is in a shady car park. Which statement is correct?
options: The sunny puddle dries first because it is warmer
The shady puddle dries first because it is cooler
The sunny puddle dries by boiling away
They dry together because they are the same size

explain.why: Cooler places slow evaporation.
The puddle does not reach boiling temperature.
The temperature differs, so the speed differs.

solution: More heat gives faster evaporation.

questions.stem: The graph shows two dishes with the same water at first. One has a lid and the other does not. Which is the dish with the lid?
options: X, because it loses very little water
Y, because it loses the most water
X, because its line starts at the top
Y, because its line falls steadily

explain.why: A lid stops water from leaving, so the lid dish loses little.
Both lines start at the same point.
A falling line means water is leaving freely.

solution: X is almost flat, so the vapour was held in by the lid.

questions.stem: The same dish of water was left at three temperatures. It took 12 hours at 20 °C, 8 hours at 30 °C and 5 hours at 40 °C to dry up. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The temperature had no effect on the time
Water dried up only at 40 °C
A higher temperature made the water dry up sooner
A higher temperature made the water last longer

explain.why: The times are all different.
It dried up at every temperature.
The time got shorter as the temperature rose.

solution: The drying time falls from 12 h to 5 h as the temperature rises.

questions.stem: Mei wants to find out if the exposed surface area affects the rate of evaporation. Which two set-ups should she compare?
options: A and D
B and D
A and B
A and C

explain.why: A and D differ in temperature.
B and D differ in both the amount of water and temperature.
A and B differ in the amount of water.

solution: A and C differ only in the dish width, which sets the exposed surface.

questions.stem: Three identical dishes hold 100 ml of water. One is uncovered in the Sun, one is uncovered in the shade and one is covered in the shade. Which line shows the dish that is uncovered in the shade?
options: M
L
K
None of them

explain.why: M is almost flat, so it is covered.
K falls fastest, so it is the one in the Sun.
The middle line fits the dish in the shade.

solution: Sun is fastest (K), shade uncovered is middle (L) and covered is slowest (M).

questions.stem: A fan blows over a tightly closed bottle of water for a whole day. The water level hardly changes. Why?
options: The moving air cools the water so much that it stops evaporating
A fan can only dry solid things
The vapour formed cannot leave the bottle
Evaporation does not happen at room temperature

explain.why: The air cannot cool the water that much. The vapour is trapped by the closed bottle.
A fan helps liquids evaporate when the vapour can leave.
It does at any temperature.

solution: A closed bottle keeps the vapour in, so the level stays almost the same.

questions.stem: A pot of water is at 25 °C. Another pot is boiling at 100 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: Water in the 25 °C pot cannot become vapour at all
Both pots evaporate, and bubbles form inside only the boiling one
Water evaporates only in the boiling pot, and not at 25 °C
Bubbles of vapour form inside both of the pots

explain.why: It slowly does.
Water at 25 °C also evaporates from its surface.
Only the boiling water has vapour bubbles throughout.

solution: Evaporation is at the surface at any temperature. Boiling also forms bubbles inside.

questions.stem: Which of the following would slow down the evaporation of seawater in a salt pan?
options: Spreading the seawater in a thin layer
Letting the wind blow across the pan
Building high walls around the pan to block the wind
Moving the pan from the shade into full sun

explain.why: A thin layer has a large surface, which speeds it up.
Wind speeds it up.
More heat speeds it up.

solution: Blocking the wind leaves vapour above the water, so evaporation is slower.

questions.stem: The three dishes hold the same amount of water and are left in the same place. Which two dishes should be compared to find the effect of exposed surface area?
options: A and C
A, B and C all together
B and C
A and B

explain.why: Compare two dishes that differ in one thing.
B and C differ in the fan only.
A and B differ in both width and fan.

solution: A and C are blown by a fan and differ only in width.

questions.stem: A dish loses 40 ml of water in 3 hours at 30 °C. The same dish, with the same amount of water, is put in the same place with the temperature raised to 40 °C. How much water does it most likely lose in 3 hours?
options: None
More than 40 ml
Exactly 40 ml
Less than 40 ml

explain.why: Water still evaporates at 40 °C.
The temperature is different, so the loss differs.
A higher temperature speeds up evaporation.

solution: Higher temperature means more water lost in the same time.

questions.stem: Which set-up in the table has the slowest rate of evaporation?
options: A
B
D
C

explain.why: A has every fast factor.
D has wind and a wide dish, so it is faster than B.
C is hot, so it is faster than B.

solution: B is cooler, has no fan and has the smallest surface.

questions.stem: Dishes P and Q differ only in width (P is 6 cm, Q is 10 cm). Dishes Q and R differ only in temperature (R is hotter). Each had 100 ml of water. The bar chart shows the water left after 3 hours. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Only the temperature changed the rate
Only the width of the dish changed the rate
A wider dish and a higher temperature each made evaporation faster
A narrower dish and a higher temperature each made evaporation faster

explain.why: Q also lost more water than P.
R also lost more water than Q.
P is narrower and kept more water.

solution: P to Q: more water lost with the wider dish. Q to R: more lost at a higher temperature.

questions.stem: Ali tests how wind affects evaporation using two dishes of water. Which of these must be kept the same in both dishes?
options: The width of the dish
The amount of water left after 3 hours
Whether a fan is blowing at the dish
The speed of the air moving over the dish

explain.why: This is what Ali measures. It is expected to differ.
This is the variable Ali changes.
This is the variable Ali changes.

solution: Everything except the wind must stay the same, including the dish width.

questions.stem: Mei changes the width of the dish to see how it affects evaporation. What should she measure?
options: The temperature of the room around the dishes
The water left in each dish after the same time
The width of each dish, which she changes
The number of dishes that she is using

explain.why: The temperature is kept the same.
She changes the width. She does not measure it as the result.
This does not show how fast the water evaporated.

solution: The result is shown by how much water has been lost in the same time.

questions.stem: A heap of wet clothes stays damp in a basket for days, but the same clothes hung out dry in a few hours. What is the main reason?
options: Little water is exposed, and air does not move over it
Clothes cannot lose water when it is dark inside
The clothes in the basket weigh less than the hung ones
The basket makes the water in the clothes more salty

explain.why: Evaporation does not need light.
Weight is not the cause.
The water does not become salty.

solution: A heap hides its water and has no wind, so it dries slowly.

questions.stem: The same volume of rainwater is spread thinly over a large car park and also collected in a narrow bucket in the same Sun. Which dries first and why?
options: The bucket, because its sides keep the water warm
They dry at the same time
The bucket, because its water is deeper than the layer
The car park, because its thin layer has a large surface

explain.why: The sides do not speed things up.
The surfaces differ greatly.
Deeper water does not dry faster.

solution: A large surface exposes more water to the air.

questions.stem: Wei pours 100 ml of water each into a narrow beaker and a wide tray in the Sun. After 2 hours, the beaker has 92 ml and the tray has 70 ml. How much more water evaporated from the tray than from the beaker?
options: 162 ml
8 ml
30 ml
22 ml

explain.why: 162 ml adds the water that is left, which is not a loss.
8 ml is the water lost from the beaker only.
30 ml is the water lost from the tray only.

solution: Tray lost 100 - 70 = 30 ml. Beaker lost 100 - 92 = 8 ml. 30 - 8 = 22 ml.

questions.stem: A dish of water dries up in 10 hours at 30 °C and in 6 hours at 40 °C. Everything else is the same. Which is the best prediction for 50 °C?
options: Exactly 2 hours
Exactly 6 hours
Less than 6 hours
More than 6 hours

explain.why: We cannot be sure of an exact time. The safe claim is that it is shorter.
Temperature has an effect.
Heat speeds up evaporation.

solution: A higher temperature makes it faster, so the time is shorter.

questions.stem: A beaker of water is placed on a hot plate that is switched on, before the water reaches boiling point. Compared with an identical beaker on a bench, what is true?
options: The beaker on the bench evaporates faster than the other
The two beakers evaporate at the same rate as each other
The beaker on the hot plate loses water faster
No water evaporates until the water starts to boil

explain.why: Heat speeds up evaporation.
The hot plate warms the water, so it evaporates faster.
Evaporation happens before boiling.

solution: Warm water evaporates faster, even before it boils.

questions.stem: Zara puts 100 ml in dish A and 150 ml in dish B, and puts a fan by B only. She wants to test the effect of the fan. How can she improve the test?
options: Use dishes of different widths
Pour equal amounts into both dishes
Put the two dishes in different places
Measure the dishes after different times

explain.why: A different width adds a second changed variable.
A different place adds a second changed variable.
Different times make the results unfair.

solution: Only the fan should differ, so the water amount must be equal.

options: Both evaporated at the same rate, but B started with less water
A did not evaporate at all
B evaporated faster because it ran out first
A evaporated faster because it has more water left

explain.why: A's line goes down, so it did evaporate.
Both lose 15 ml each hour.
More water left does not mean faster loss.

solution: Both lines have the same steepness: 15 ml per hour.

20 hours
Exactly 8 hours
Fewer than 8 hours

explain.why: The time falls as the dish gets wider.
20 hours is for the narrowest dish.
The pattern is that wider dishes dry sooner.

solution: Wider dishes dry up sooner, so 12 cm takes less than 8 hours.

P
Q
S

explain.why: R lost some water, but S lost more.
P has the most water left, so it was probably the coolest.
Q lost some water, but S lost more.

solution: S lost the most water (85 ml), so it evaporated fastest.

questions.stem: Which of the following is water in its solid state?
options: A puddle
A hailstone
A raindrop
Water vapour in the air

explain.why: A puddle is liquid water.
A raindrop is liquid water.
Water vapour is the gas state.

solution: A hailstone is a lump of ice, which is solid water.

questions.stem: Which statement about water in the gas state is correct?
options: It cannot be seen and has no fixed shape
It can be seen and has a fixed volume always
It has a fixed shape and can be seen easily
It has a fixed shape and a fixed volume

explain.why: Water vapour cannot be seen and it spreads out.
Water vapour is invisible and has no shape of its own.
That describes a solid, such as ice.

solution: Water vapour is invisible and spreads out to fill the space it is in.

questions.stem: Which state of water keeps its own shape?
options: Ice
Liquid water
Water vapour
Both liquid water and water vapour

explain.why: Liquid water takes the shape of its container.
Water vapour spreads out in any space.
Neither of these keeps its own shape.

solution: Only the solid state, ice, has a fixed shape.

questions.stem: Which state of water takes the shape of its container but keeps the same volume?
options: All three states of water
Ice
Water vapour
Liquid water

explain.why: Ice does not take the shape of its container.
Ice keeps its own shape.
Water vapour also changes its volume to fill the space.

solution: A liquid can flow into the shape of a container, and its volume stays the same.

questions.stem: Which letter in the diagram shows ice changing into water?
options: S
P
Q
R

explain.why: S is water vapour changing into water.
Q is water changing into ice, which is freezing.
R is water changing into water vapour.

solution: Ice to water is melting, which is P.

options: S
P
Q
R

explain.why: P is melting.
Q is freezing.
R is water changing into a gas, the opposite of condensation.

solution: Condensation is water vapour changing into liquid water, which is S.

questions.stem: What is the change from liquid water to ice called?
options: Melting
Condensation
Boiling
Freezing

explain.why: Melting is ice changing into water.
Condensation is a gas changing into a liquid.
Boiling is water changing into a gas.

solution: Liquid water changes to ice when it freezes.

questions.stem: What is the change from water vapour to liquid water called?
options: Melting
Freezing
Evaporation or boiling
Condensation

explain.why: Melting is ice changing into water.
Freezing is water changing into ice.
Evaporation is liquid water changing into water vapour.

solution: A gas changing to a liquid is condensation.

questions.stem: At which temperature does pure ice melt?

explain.why: 37 °C is the temperature of a healthy body.
100 °C is the boiling point of water.
Ice that is already melting is not this cold.

solution: Ice melts at 0 °C.

questions.stem: At which temperature does pure water boil at sea level?

explain.why: This is a cold temperature.
Water is not boiling yet at 90 °C.
0 °C is the melting point of ice.

solution: Water boils at 100 °C.

questions.stem: Ice cubes on a plate in a warm room turn into water. What happens to the ice?
options: It gains heat and melts
It loses heat and freezes
It loses heat and melts
It gains heat and freezes

explain.why: The ice is turning into water, not the other way round.
Melting needs heat to be gained.
Freezing is the change from water to ice.

solution: The ice takes in heat from the warm room and melts.

questions.stem: Droplets of water form on the outside of a glass of iced water. Where does the water come from?
options: Water vapour in the air
Ice that melts and flows out of the glass
The glass itself, which makes water when cold
Water that leaks through the glass

explain.why: The glass is not leaking.
A glass cannot make water.
Glass has no holes for water to pass through.

solution: Water vapour in the air touches the cold glass and condenses.

questions.stem: A puddle on a concrete floor slowly disappears on a sunny day. What has happened to the water?
options: It has changed into water vapour in the air
It has been used up and is gone for good
It has soaked down into the concrete floor
It has frozen into a thin sheet of ice on the floor

explain.why: Water does not disappear. It changes state.
Concrete floors do not soak up this much water.
The Sun makes things warm, so ice would not form.

solution: The water gains heat from the Sun and evaporates.

questions.stem: A kettle of water is boiling. What is the white mist at Y made of?
options: Smoke from the burning heater
Tiny drops of liquid water
Water vapour coming out of the spout
Tiny pieces of ice

explain.why: The kettle only contains water.
Water vapour is a gas that we cannot see.
The air above a kettle is too hot for ice.

solution: Water vapour cools in the air and condenses into tiny drops, which we see as mist.

P
Q
R

25 °C is below the melting point of Q, so Q is solid.
25 °C is above the boiling point of R, so R is a gas.

solution: A liquid is above its melting point and below its boiling point. 25 °C is between -20 °C and 80 °C.

questions.stem: Ice at -5 °C is heated in a beaker. What is the first change seen when the ice reaches 0 °C?
options: The ice turns into water vapour
The water begins to boil
The ice begins to melt
The water begins to freeze

explain.why: Ice becomes liquid first.
Boiling happens much later, at 100 °C.
Heating cannot make water freeze.

solution: At 0 °C the ice starts to melt.

questions.stem: Which states of water can flow?
options: Ice and liquid water
Liquid water and water vapour
Ice, which can be poured out
Water vapour only, since it spreads out

explain.why: Ice does not flow.
Ice keeps its shape and does not flow.
Liquid water can flow too.

solution: Liquids and gases can flow, but solids cannot.

questions.stem: Water in an ice tray is put in a freezer and turns into ice. What happens to the water?
options: It loses heat and melts
It gains heat and freezes
It gains heat and melts
It loses heat and freezes

explain.why: Melting is ice becoming water.
Water must lose heat to freeze.
The water is becoming ice, not melting.

solution: Water gives out heat to the cold freezer and becomes ice.

questions.stem: A bathroom mirror becomes misty after a hot shower. Which change caused this?
options: Water on the mirror freezing into ice
Hot water melting on the mirror
Water vapour condensing on the cool mirror
Water vapour boiling away on the mirror

explain.why: The mirror is not cold enough to make ice.
Melting is ice turning into water.
Boiling needs the water to gain heat.

solution: Water vapour from the shower loses heat to the cool mirror and condenses into tiny droplets.

questions.stem: Which state of water can be squeezed into a smaller space most easily?
options: Liquid water
Ice
Ice and liquid water
Water vapour

explain.why: A liquid is hard to squeeze smaller.
A solid is hard to squeeze smaller.
Neither can be squeezed easily.

solution: A gas can be squeezed into a smaller space.

questions.stem: The water in a beaker is bubbling and the thermometer reading is shown. What does the reading tell us?
options: Water freezes at this temperature
Water melts at this temperature
The water is not yet hot enough to boil
Water boils at this temperature

explain.why: Water freezes at 0 °C.
Ice melts at 0 °C.
The reading is at the boiling point.

solution: The reading is 100 °C, the boiling point of water.

questions.stem: Ice, liquid water and water vapour are ____.
options: three states of the same substance
three different kinds of substance
three kinds of water that never change into each other
three kinds of liquid

explain.why: They are all water.
Ice is solid, water is liquid and vapour is a gas.
Only one of them is a liquid.

solution: They are the solid, liquid and gas states of water.

questions.stem: Wet clothes dry on a clothes line. What has happened to the water in the clothes?
options: It has frozen into ice
It has changed into water vapour
It has disappeared completely
It has changed into ice and then melted

explain.why: The clothes are not cold enough for ice.
Water does not vanish. It changes state.
No ice forms when clothes dry in the air.

solution: The water in the clothes evaporates into the air.

questions.stem: Which two letters in the diagram show changes in which water gains heat?
options: Q and S
R and S
P and Q
P and R

explain.why: Freezing and condensation need heat to be lost.
S is condensation, which needs heat to be lost.
Q is freezing, which needs heat to be lost.

solution: Melting (P) and boiling or evaporation (R) both need heat to be gained.

questions.stem: Droplets form on the outside of a glass of iced water. Why does this happen?
options: Water from the ice seeps through the glass
Water vapour in the air loses heat to the cold glass and condenses
Water vapour in the air gains heat from the glass and condenses
Cold from the ice goes through the glass and freezes the air

explain.why: Glass does not let water through.
Condensing needs heat to be lost.
Cold does not flow. Heat is lost from the air to the glass.

solution: Warm air next to the cold glass loses heat, so water vapour condenses into droplets.

Tiny pieces of ice

options: Ice forms in the air away from the spout
The water has not yet boiled near the spout
The vapour only condenses after it has cooled in the air
The vapour changes into liquid before it leaves

explain.why: The mist is liquid drops, not ice.
The water is boiling because vapour is coming out.
Condensation would wet the spout instead of leaving a gap.

solution: Hot vapour is invisible. It cools in the air and condenses into mist a little way out.

questions.stem: A cold lid is held over a pot of boiling water. Droplets form under the lid. Why?
options: Hot water boils on the lid and falls back as drops
The rising vapour gives out heat to the lid and condenses
The lid has tiny holes that let water out
The rising vapour takes in heat from the lid and condenses

explain.why: Boiling needs the water to gain heat, and the lid is cold.
The droplets are on the underside, so they come from below.
Condensation needs heat to be lost.

solution: Water vapour rising from the pot meets the cold lid, loses heat and turns into liquid drops.

options: Q
S
P
R

explain.why: 20 °C is between -39 °C and 357 °C, so Q is a liquid.
20 °C is between -115 °C and 78 °C, so P is a liquid.
20 °C is below the melting point of R, so R is a solid.

solution: 20 °C is above the boiling point of S (-183 °C), so S is a gas.

questions.stem: A block of ice at 0 °C is placed in a warm room. What happens to the temperature of the ice while it is melting?
options: It rises steadily as the room is warm
It falls below 0 °C as the ice loses cold
It stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted
It rises to 100 °C at once

explain.why: The temperature stays at the melting point until the ice is gone.
The ice gains heat from the room. It does not get colder.
Only boiling water reaches 100 °C.

solution: The heat gained is used to melt the ice, so the temperature stays at 0 °C.

questions.stem: Water in an open beaker is boiling on a stove. The thermometer stays at 100 °C even though the flame is still on. What is the heat being used for?
options: Making the beaker lose mass
Changing liquid water into water vapour
Making the water hotter than 100 °C
Turning water vapour back into liquid water

explain.why: The heat is used to change the water's state.
The reading is not rising.
That change gives out heat.

solution: The heat is used to change water into water vapour, not to raise the temperature.

questions.stem: On a cool morning the inside of a bus window is covered with tiny drops. What are the drops?
options: Ice that has melted from the window glass
Water that has leaked through the glass from outside
Liquid water formed from water vapour in the passengers' breath
Water vapour that has become visible

explain.why: The glass is not made of ice.
The drops form on the inside, from the warm moist air.
Water vapour cannot be seen. The drops are liquid.

solution: Water vapour from breath cools on the cold glass and condenses into liquid drops.

questions.stem: Which statement about boiling and evaporation is correct?
options: Boiling happens only at the surface, but evaporation happens throughout the water
Evaporation needs the water to lose heat
Evaporation happens only at the surface, but boiling happens throughout the water
Both happen only when water is at 100 °C

explain.why: Bubbles form inside boiling water.
Both changes need heat to be gained.
Evaporation also happens at lower temperatures.

solution: Evaporation takes place at the surface at any temperature. Boiling takes place throughout the liquid at 100 °C.

questions.stem: The table describes water in three forms X, Y and Z. Which one is water vapour?
options: Both X and Y
Z
Y
X

explain.why: Neither of them spreads out to fill a space.
Y takes any shape but keeps its volume, so it is liquid water.
X has a fixed shape and a fixed volume, so it is ice.

solution: Water vapour has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.
