questions.stem: Which of the following changes needs water to lose heat?
options: A wet floor drying in the hot Sun
Water bubbling away in a hot pot
Water vapour forming drops on a cold window
An ice cube turning into water in a cup

explain.why: Drying means water gains heat and evaporates.
Boiling needs heat to be gained.
Melting needs heat to be gained.

solution: Condensation is the only change here in which water loses heat.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes boiling?
options: Liquid water changes to water vapour throughout the liquid at 100 °C
Water vapour changes to liquid water on cooling at 100 °C
Ice changes to liquid water throughout the block at 100 °C
Liquid water changes to ice throughout the liquid at 0 °C

explain.why: That is condensation.
That describes melting, which happens at 0 °C.
That is freezing.

solution: Boiling is the change from liquid to gas, happening in the whole liquid at 100 °C.

questions.stem: A beaker of water at 15 °C is put in a freezer. The thermometer shows the same reading for a long time while the water turns into ice. What is the reading?

explain.why: The water has cooled well below its starting temperature.
That is the boiling point.
That is the freezer's temperature, reached only after all the water has frozen.

solution: Water freezes at 0 °C, and its temperature stays there until all of it is ice.

questions.stem: A student pours 200 mL of water from a jug into a tall glass, and then into a wide bowl. Which statement is correct?
options: The shape of the water changes but its volume stays at 200 mL
Neither the shape nor the volume of the water changes
Both the shape and the volume of the water change
The shape of the water stays the same but its volume changes

explain.why: The shape follows the container.
The amount of water stays the same.
Liquid water takes the shape of its container.

solution: A liquid takes the shape of its container and keeps its volume.

questions.stem: On a hot day an ice lolly melts and drips. What happens to heat?
options: The lolly loses heat to the air
No heat moves, since the lolly is cold
The air gains heat from the lolly
The lolly gains heat from the air

explain.why: Melting needs heat to be gained.
A difference in temperature always makes heat flow.
Heat flows from the hot air to the cold lolly.

solution: Heat flows from the warm air to the cold lolly, which melts.

questions.stem: The temperature at which pure liquid water changes into a gas is called the ____ point.
options: boiling
condensing
freezing
melting

explain.why: Condensation is the change from gas to liquid.
Freezing is the change from liquid to solid.
Melting is the change from solid to liquid.

solution: Water changes to a gas at its boiling point, 100 °C.

questions.stem: Ice cubes at 0 °C are put into hot tea at 80 °C and the tea is stirred until all the ice has melted. Which describes the final temperature of the tea?
options: Between 0 °C and 80 °C
Above 80 °C, as heat was added
Exactly 80 °C, as it was before
Exactly 0 °C, the same as the ice

explain.why: The tea cannot become hotter by adding ice.
The tea loses some heat to the ice, so it cools.
There was much more heat in the hot tea than the ice needed.

solution: The tea loses heat to the ice, which melts and warms up, so the final temperature is between 0 °C and 80 °C.

questions.stem: Mei Ling wants to find out how the mass of ice affects the time it takes to melt in a warm room. Which is the measured variable?
options: The mass of ice put in each beaker
The temperature of the warm room
The time taken for the ice to melt
The type of container that is used

explain.why: This is the variable she changes on purpose.
This should be kept the same.
This should be kept the same.

solution: She changes the mass and measures the time taken.

questions.stem: A beaker of crushed ice and water is left on a warm table. The thermometer in the beaker is read every minute while some ice is still left. What does it show?
options: A reading that slowly rises above 0 °C
A reading that rises to the room temperature at once
A reading of 0 °C all the time
A reading that falls below 0 °C

explain.why: Heat from the room melts the ice instead of warming it.
While ice remains, the mixture stays at 0 °C.
The ice is gaining heat, not losing it.

solution: The heat gained is used to melt ice, so the temperature stays at 0 °C until the ice is gone.

questions.stem: More droplets form on the outside of a cold can on a very humid day than on a dry day. Why?
options: More ice melts inside the can
The air is hotter and gives more heat to the can
The can makes more water from the cold
The air has more water vapour that can condense

explain.why: The droplets come from outside the can.
Heat gained by the can does not make droplets.
A can cannot make water.

solution: More water vapour in the air means more of it condenses on the cold can.

questions.stem: A girl walks from an air-conditioned room into the warm, humid air outside. Her spectacles become covered with a fine mist. Why?
options: Water vapour in her breath freezes on the lenses
Water vapour in the warm air condenses on the cold lenses
The lenses make water when they warm up
Water inside the lenses boils away to the surface

explain.why: The lenses are cold, but not below 0 °C.
Glass cannot make water.
Glass does not contain water.

solution: The lenses are cooler than the air, so water vapour touching them loses heat and condenses.

questions.stem: Two cans in a 30 °C room each hold water. Can A has iced water. Can B has water at 30 °C. Droplets form only on Can A. Why?
options: Can B has no water vapour in the air around it
Can A gives out more heat to the room than Can B does
The water in Can B has already evaporated and boiled away
The surface of A is cold enough to make water vapour lose heat

explain.why: Both cans are surrounded by the same air.
Can A is colder, so it gains heat.
Water at 30 °C does not boil.

solution: Only the cold surface cools the nearby air enough for water vapour to condense.

questions.stem: A sealed bottle of iced water is weighed before and after droplets form on its outside. The total mass has gone up. What does this show?
options: The water in the droplets came from the air
The water in the droplets came from inside the bottle
The ice in the bottle became heavier as it got colder
The ice in the bottle melted into the droplets

explain.why: The mass would not go up if water only moved from inside the bottle.
Water drops have mass.
The bottle is sealed, so melting ice stays inside.

solution: Extra mass can only come from outside the sealed bottle, so the droplets came from water vapour in the air.

questions.stem: Aisha wants to find out whether the starting temperature of the water affects how fast an ice cube melts. Which set-up is a fair test?
options: Two beakers of 100 mL of water at 20 °C and 40 °C, each with an identical ice cube
One beaker of water at 20 °C tested for a long time and another tested for a short time
Two beakers of water at 20 °C and 40 °C, with one ice cube and one crushed ice
A beaker of 100 mL of water at 20 °C and a beaker of 200 mL of water at 40 °C

explain.why: The time is not the thing to be changed.
The ice differs, so more than one thing changes.
The amount of water also changes.

solution: Only the starting temperature of the water is changed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true for ice, liquid water and water vapour?
options: They all have a fixed volume that never changes
They all can flow from one container to another
They all have mass and take up space
They all keep their own shape in any container

explain.why: Water vapour spreads out to fill its container.
Ice does not flow.
Only ice keeps its own shape.

solution: All three are matter, so they have mass and take up space.

questions.stem: A tube of each substance is placed in a water bath at 100 °C. Which substance that is a liquid at 20 °C will boil?
options: P
Q
S
R

explain.why: Q boils at 357 °C, far above 100 °C.
S is already a gas at 20 °C, so it is not a liquid.
R is a solid at 20 °C and boils at 2750 °C.

solution: Only P is a liquid at 20 °C with a boiling point (78 °C) below 100 °C.

questions.stem: The table shows the melting points and boiling points of four substances. Which substance is a liquid at -100 °C?
options: R
Q
P
S

explain.why: -100 °C is below the melting point of R, so R is solid.
-100 °C is below the melting point of Q, so Q is solid.
-100 °C is above the boiling point of S, so S is a gas.

solution: -100 °C is between -115 °C and 78 °C, so P is a liquid.

questions.stem: A student holds a cold metal plate above the spout at X in the kettle. Drops of water form on the plate. What does this show about X?
options: Only air is present there
Ice is present there
Tiny drops of water are already there
Water vapour is present there

explain.why: The drops need a supply of water.
The air at the spout is too hot for ice.
If drops were there, X would look misty.

solution: Invisible water vapour cooled and condensed on the cold plate.

questions.stem: Few droplets form under the lid when it is warmed to 100 °C before it is placed over the pot of boiling water. Why?
options: The water in the pot has stopped boiling
The warm lid gives heat to the water vapour, which then freezes
The warm lid makes the water vapour disappear
The warm lid does not take enough heat from the water vapour

explain.why: The pot is still boiling.
Water vapour does not freeze at this temperature.
Water vapour is still there but is not condensing.

solution: Condensation needs the water vapour to lose heat to a cooler surface.

explain.why: 8 is a time in minutes, not a temperature.
90 °C is only the final reading.
30 °C is the starting temperature.

solution: The temperature stays at 60 °C while the wax melts.

options: Liquid and gas, since it is very hot
Solid wax only, not yet changed
Liquid wax only, all melted by now
Partly solid and partly liquid

explain.why: The wax has not started to boil.
The wax started to melt at 3 minutes.
The wax is still melting.

solution: The flat part from 3 to 8 minutes is the wax melting, so solid and liquid are both present.

options: S, then Q
P, then R
R, then P
Q, then S

explain.why: P is condensation and R is freezing.
R is freezing and P is condensation.
Q is boiling or evaporation, which comes after melting.

solution: Ice melts first, which is S. The water then evaporates, which is Q.

It rises steadily to room temperature
It rises to 0 °C and stays there until the ice has melted

solution: Water vapour is an invisible gas that is always in the air.

The ice loses heat as fast as it gains heat

questions.stem: Ice is heated in a beaker and its temperature is recorded as shown. In which state is the water at 3 minutes?
options: Liquid water and water vapour
Ice and liquid water
Ice only
Liquid water only

explain.why: The water does not boil until about 12 minutes.
The ice has started to melt after 2 minutes.
The ice does not finish melting until 6 minutes.

solution: At 3 minutes the graph is in the flat part B at 0 °C, so ice and liquid water are both there.

questions.stem: Ice is heated in a beaker and its temperature is recorded as shown. What can be seen in the beaker at 15 minutes?
options: Water with no bubbles, which is still getting hotter
Only ice cubes still floating in cold water
Bubbles rising through water that is still there
Only clear gas, with no liquid water left

explain.why: Water at 100 °C is boiling, so it has bubbles.
The ice melted by 6 minutes.
The water has not all boiled away yet.

solution: At 15 minutes the water is boiling at 100 °C, so there are bubbles and liquid is left.
